questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why the empire could not be held
questions.learningObjective: Explain why thin metropolitan staffing made empire fragile.
questions.stem: Your transect notes record that a colonial administration staffed its outposts at one official per forty kilometres, relying on village headmen for daily order. Which explanation best fits why the empire could not hold the territory?

options.text: Local rulers carried the cost, so the empire rested on intermediaries whose loyalty was negotiable.
The imperial army was technically incapable of moving between the two river systems.
options.misconception: believes the empire failed for purely technical reasons

options.text: European settlers in the interior opposed the imperial presence and worked to end it.
options.misconception: believes settlers were the main agents of the empire's collapse

options.text: Trading firms paid more in customs duties than the territory cost to administer.
options.misconception: believes customs duties exceeded the cost of administration

questions.explanation: Colonial rule was cheap because local rulers carried the administrative weight, so the empire rested on negotiable intermediaries. Logistics, settlers and customs revenue do not explain the weakness.
questions.hint: Ask who really carried the cost of governing.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Infer how land distribution shaped rural grievance in the highlands.
questions.stem: A land survey you are auditing compares white settlement and African landholding in the Kenyan highlands in 1950: settler farms occupied 3,100 square kilometres with 62,000 hectares cultivated, while African holdings covered 9,400 square kilometres with only 24,000 hectares cultivated. Which inference is best supported?

options.text: African farmers cultivated more land per square kilometre than settler farms did.
options.misconception: inverts the ratio of cultivation between the two groups

options.text: Settler farms were less intensively farmed, so African land was underused by comparison.
options.misconception: reads the higher settler yield as evidence African land was idle

options.text: Land distribution favoured settlers, giving African farmers less cultivated ground per area.
Total farm numbers were equal on both sides, so the difference lay only in farm size.
options.misconception: assumes the difference lay only in the size of individual farms

questions.explanation: Settlers held a minority of the area but nearly three times the cultivated hectares, so the imbalance in usable land worked against African farmers. Cultivation per square kilometre was higher for settlers.
questions.hint: Compare cultivated hectares, not just land area.

questions.stem: Your survey route passes through the straits guarding the Indian Ocean. You must explain why control of these waters mattered so much to imperial strategists in the twentieth century.

options.misconception: reduces the straits' importance to mail volumes

options.text: They mattered chiefly as the site of the earliest European trading settlements in Asia.
options.misconception: claims early European settlement explains their value

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why independence left the island economy apparently unchanged.
questions.stem: Your survey report on a Caribbean plantation island asks you to explain why the island's economy looked almost unchanged after the transfer of sovereignty in the nineteen-sixties.

answer.exemplar: Independence changed the flag, the legal personality of the state and the diplomatic representation abroad, but the island's export earnings still came from the same crops shipped to the same markets under the same ownership of land and processing plants. The new government's revenue base, credit arrangements and foreign trading partners were largely inherited from the colonial period, so political sovereignty was real while the structure that produced income stayed as it was.

questions.explanation: Political sovereignty changed while ownership, crops and trading partners did not, so the economic structure of the island survived the transfer intact. New flags and new diplomatic representation did not alter the plantation economy.
questions.hint: Focus on ownership and export markets rather than sovereignty.

questions.learningObjective: Interpret a coup report as an assertion of continuity and order.

stimulus.body: Following the morning's troop movements, a proclamation from the new command states that the previous government was unable to govern and that order is being restored. questions.stem: An archive label accompanies this report from a coup. Which reading of the new regime's claim to legitimacy does the evidence support?

options.text: The regime has established its legitimacy by securing a broad popular mandate.
options.misconception: reads normal administration as proof of popular consent

options.text: The regime has replaced the old state with a fully civilian administration.
options.misconception: assumes a civilian administration replaced the previous one

options.text: The regime is asserting legitimacy through continuity and order rather than consent.
The regime has obtained recognition from the metropolitan government it replaced.
options.misconception: assumes metropolitan recognition was already granted

questions.explanation: The proclamation claims a vacuum and the report shows administration continuing, so legitimacy rests on presenting the coup as order restored, not on consent. Mandate, civilian rule and recognition are not evidenced.
questions.hint: Note what the report says about markets and taxes.

questions.learningObjective: Weigh the factors that sustained a late colonial war.
questions.stem: A field station's history panel must explain why one European power's empire survived into the nineteen-seventies while others dissolved. Which combination of factors best accounts for that difference?

options.text: A low-cost war of attrition, firm metropolitan resolve and material support from a superpower.
A large professional army, modern weapons and the absence of any local resistance.
options.misconception: credits endurance to military strength and denies local resistance

options.text: Rich colonial reserves, a prosperous metropolitan economy and an early grant of independence.
options.misconception: invents reserves and metropolitan wealth as the explanation

options.text: Successful mediation by neighbours, a planned handover and regional consent to remain.
options.misconception: invents negotiated handover and regional consent as the explanation

questions.explanation: The resistance held out because the war was cheap to sustain, the metropolitan government refused to concede, and superpower support supplied weapons. Local resistance existed, and no handover was negotiated.
questions.hint: Weigh cost, resolve and outside support together.

options.misconception: assumes road quality explains differences in control

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how land classification became the central grievance of a rebellion.
questions.stem: Your transect notebook asks you to explain why colonial land policy turned a routine question of ownership into the central grievance of a rebellion in the highlands.

answer.exemplar: European settlement was justified by classifying African-held country as unused, while communities who had farmed the same ground for generations were described as having no rights in it. When enclosures and the compulsory labour levy followed, the dispute was no longer about policy but about survival: families had lost the land they worked and the labour they owed themselves. That combination turned a legal classification into the spark of organised resistance.

questions.explanation: Enclosure removed land while the labour levy took the time that sustained farming, so a legal classification became a survival struggle. That combination explains the scale of the resistance.
questions.hint: Consider what families lost beyond the ground itself.

options.text: The new state had signed new trade agreements that replaced the old preference deal.
options.misconception: claims new trade agreements replaced the preference agreement

options.text: The new state had deliberately abandoned the old shipping and insurance networks.
options.misconception: claims the old networks were deliberately abandoned

options.text: The new state had gained sovereignty in law while keeping its colonial economic structure.

questions.explanation: The note lists the same shipping, insurance, brokers, single crop and preference agreement beside new trappings: sovereignty in law with the colonial economy intact. Diversification and new agreements are contradicted.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Weigh inheritance against choice in explaining economic continuity.
questions.stem: A research seminar in your field station asks you to weigh two explanations for the persistence of plantation economies after independence: one about colonial inheritance, one about the choices new governments made. Which combined judgement is most defensible?

options.text: Inherited structures left no choices at all, so governments bore no responsibility for the outcome.
options.misconception: claims inherited structures removed all meaningful choice

options.text: Governments had wide freedom and chose continuity because they had no interest in change.
options.misconception: claims wide freedom alongside an inexplicable lack of interest

options.text: The two explanations are equally weak, since the outcome is largely unexplained by either.
options.misconception: dismisses both explanations without offering a third

options.text: Inherited structures narrowed the choices, and governments then chose which burdens to keep.

questions.explanation: Colonial landholding and export arrangements narrowed the options, and governments decided which inherited burdens to keep and which to renegotiate. Choices were constrained but real, and continuity had political causes.

options.text: The insurgency was winning, since it had taken most of the country by the end of the year.
options.misconception: reads a shrinking rebel area as a rebel victory

options.text: The government had crushed the insurgency, since the insurgents were confined to a few districts.
options.misconception: claims the insurgency was crushed by government forces

options.misconception: claims the two sides reached a stable stalemate

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why redistributing land alone did not end rural poverty.
questions.stem: Your land-use survey asks why a revolutionary land reform that redistributed land could still leave rural poverty and political instability behind.

options.text: Because the reform gave land to households that had never farmed, so yields collapsed.
options.misconception: blames the reform on inexperienced new landholders alone

options.text: Because the reform was administered by colonial officials who refused to implement it.
options.misconception: blames the reform on colonial officials refusing to implement it

options.text: Because the reform created large state farms that needed heavy credit to operate.
options.misconception: blames the reform on the creation of large state farms

options.text: Because titles without credit, tools or markets left many new owners unable to prosper.

questions.explanation: Redistribution changed ownership without changing the surrounding economy, so new holders faced the same credit and market problems as before. Inexperience and state farms are possible flaws, not the pattern.
questions.hint: Ask what changed and what stayed the same.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how temporary migration reshaped the politics of receiving states.
questions.stem: Your survey handbook asks you to explain how a migration that began as a temporary labour arrangement reshaped the politics of the receiving societies.

answer.exemplar: Temporary recruitment on a large scale left workers, families and employers all expecting continuity, so when the workers stayed their demands for housing, schooling, wages and the vote could not be deferred indefinitely. Governments that had treated the newcomers as a labour reserve found themselves obliged to answer claims of citizenship and belonging, which in turn transformed party politics and the definition of national identity in the receiving states.

questions.explanation: A temporary arrangement that produced permanent residents created lasting claims to services and citizenship, which reshaped party politics in the receiving states. The direction and scale of the effect cannot be read from the numbers alone.
questions.hint: Focus on what permanence forced governments to concede.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a guerrilla war could stalemate for years.
questions.stem: Your station's public history piece must explain why an anti-colonial war in the region dragged on for years after comparable wars elsewhere had ended.

answer.exemplar: The metropolitan state had decided that withdrawal would be a humiliation it could not afford, so it kept a war running in the hope that a favourable political turn would let it win. Because the fighting was fought by a small, thinly supplied guerrilla force in difficult terrain, the colonial side could not achieve the decisive victory that would have ended it, and every year of stalemate cost the rebels little while tying down the metropolitan budget and political will.

questions.explanation: Metropolitan refusal to concede and the impossibility of decisive victory for a small guerrilla force explain the stalemate. The war continued because neither side could achieve the outcome its strategy required.
questions.hint: Ask what each side's strategy prevented it from achieving.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why new political elites emerged without new economic ones.
questions.stem: Your field station's comparative brief asks you to explain why Caribbean independence so often produced new political elites without producing new economic ones.

answer.exemplar: Political offices multiplied with the constitution, the assembly and the new diplomatic service, so men who had once been organisers, teachers and union organisers could take up careers in the state that the old regime would never have offered them. Economic power sat elsewhere, in the export houses, the shipping agents, the banks and the large landowners, whose positions rested on leases and contracts inherited from the colony. Competitions for office were therefore reopened even where control of income was not.

questions.explanation: New political posts opened careers that colonial rule had closed, while economic power stayed with those holding inherited assets. Recreating a political class therefore did not mean redistributing economic power.
questions.hint: Focus on which careers opened and which assets did not move.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why enclosure was experienced as a moral wrong.
questions.stem: Your field station's teaching material asks you to explain why the enclosure of African land was experienced as a moral wrong rather than merely as a change in land management.

answer.exemplar: Officials described the enclosures as tidying land that nobody used, but the communities losing it knew exactly who had grazed it, who had cleared it and for how long. The loss of grazing, of burial grounds and of the right to settle in the face of drought was a loss of the family's place in a landscape, not a change in a rent book. Where compensation was refused and the new farms enclosed the water sources as well as the fields, the dispossession became the memory that later movements drew on.

questions.explanation: Enclosure removed land communities had used for generations and refused compensation, so the change was experienced as dispossession of a place rather than tidying. The legal description and the lived experience diverged sharply.
questions.hint: Focus on what was lost that was not in the accounts.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why temporary recruitment reshaped national politics.
questions.stem: Your station's education material asks you to explain why the politics of the receiving states changed once temporary workers became a settled population.

answer.exemplar: The temporary worker was a labour input to be regulated and counted; the settled worker was a voter, a parent and a claim on housing. Once recruitment created neighbourhoods where children were born and schools were needed, governments could no longer treat the population as a revolving labour supply. questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how domestic debate constrained what could be negotiated.
questions.stem: Your station's public history note asks you to explain how a colonial power's own debate about the war shaped the terms it was willing to discuss.

answer.exemplar: A metropolitan government fighting an expensive war had to answer for it at home, and the terms it could accept were shaped by what it had already told its public. A government that had described the conflict as a matter of order and obligation could not then hand the territory over without appearing to concede that the whole campaign had been unnecessary, so it insisted on agreements about future status and about the safety of its own nationals. The politics at home thus narrowed what was negotiable, and the war continued longer than a purely strategic calculation would have required.

questions.explanation: Public commitments shaped what a government could concede without appearing to reverse itself, which limited the range of available terms and prolonged the war. Military logic alone did not determine the outcome.
questions.hint: Focus on what the government had already told its public.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why office was easier to redistribute than property.
questions.stem: A teaching session asks you to explain why Caribbean governments found it easier to change who held public office than to change who owned the export estates.

answer.exemplar: Public office was a scarce resource that an independent administration had to fill from scratch, and the first governments took the available positions for themselves and their supporters, a change visible in a single parliament. The export estates, by contrast, were held under titles, leases and credit arrangements written in the colonial period, and untangling them required either compensation the treasury did not have or confrontation with owners who controlled the ports and the customs revenue. Independence could redistribute positions; it could not easily redistribute property.

questions.explanation: Public posts could be refilled from scratch, whereas property rights were embedded in colonial titles and credit arrangements that the new state could not afford to undo. Office and property required different instruments.

It adds that the district administrator has been replaced and that the committee has asked for the allocation of a vehicle and a fuel allowance.

questions.stem: An exhibit uses this provincial report from a military-governed district. What does the evidence show about how the regime consolidated its authority?

options.text: The regime combined local intermediaries, surveillance and material inducements.
The regime had dismantled the previous administration entirely within one quarter.
options.misconception: reads one personnel change as the abolition of an administration

options.text: The regime had handed day-to-day administration to elected local representatives.
options.misconception: confuses naming attendance lists with elected representation

options.text: The regime depended on outside aid agencies to carry out local government.
options.misconception: attributes local government to outside aid agencies

questions.explanation: Attendance lists, a replaced administrator and requests for vehicles and fuel show a regime keeping local structures, monitoring them and buying cooperation with resources. Abolition, elections and reliance on aid agencies are not in the evidence.
questions.hint: Ask what the lists, the car and the appointment show together.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Weigh the domestic political legacy of a long colonial war.
questions.stem: A seminar asks how the experience of a long colonial war shaped the political outlook of the metropolitan country afterwards.

options.text: The war produced a durable conviction that overseas commitments were affordable and beneficial.
options.misconception: claims the war confirmed metropolitan confidence in empire

options.text: The war left a lasting mark on political debate, so later governments approached commitments differently.
The war left politics unchanged, because military campaigns rarely affect domestic arguments.
options.misconception: claims military campaigns have no domestic political effect

options.text: The war was largely forgotten at home, since its costs fell on the colonies rather than the metropole.
options.misconception: claims the war's costs were borne outside the metropole

questions.explanation: An expensive war with heavy domestic opposition left a lasting mark on political debate, so later governments approached overseas commitments differently. Empire was neither embraced without cost nor forgotten, and campaigns do affect domestic argument.
questions.hint: Ask what the war cost at home politically.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Identify the measure that shows a reform changed rural power.
questions.stem: Your agrarian brief asks you to identify the measure that best shows whether a land reform actually changed rural power rather than just rural paperwork.

options.text: Whether the villages' leading offices and councils changed hands along with the land.
The number of certificates of title issued in the first year of the reform.
options.misconception: treats a count of title certificates as evidence of changed power

options.text: The total acreage transferred to new owners within five years.
options.misconception: treats transferred acreage as sufficient evidence of changed power

options.text: The speed with which the land commission published its decisions.
options.misconception: treats administrative speed as the measure of political change

questions.explanation: Power follows the offices that direct village business, so who held them after the reform reveals whether the change was more than legal. Certificate counts, acreage and administrative speed describe scale, not political reach.
questions.hint: Ask who held the offices afterwards.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Infer which public services kept pace with a migrant population.
questions.stem: A municipal accounts summary you are checking lists spending per 1,000 residents in one receiving town between 1960 and 1975: schools rose from 31 to 44 units, municipal housing from 18 to 29, and health services from 12 to 13, while the town's population grew by a third. Which inference is best supported?

options.text: Schools and housing absorbed the growth in demand while health spending lagged behind.
Health spending grew faster than schools, because the figures show a clear priority.
options.misconception: claims health spending outpaced the other categories

options.text: All three services kept pace with population growth, so nothing was left behind.
options.misconception: assumes every service kept pace with population growth

options.text: Spending fell in every category, so the town's services must have contracted.
options.misconception: assumes spending fell across all categories

questions.explanation: Schools and housing rose faster than population while health spending was nearly flat, so the town met part of the new demand and left part unmet. Health did not outpace the rest, and no category fell.
questions.hint: Compare each category with the growth in population.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why the empire could not be held
questions.learningObjective: Explain why metropolitan willingness to concede varied between territories.
questions.stem: Your seminar asks why the imperial centre's willingness to concede varied so sharply between territories in the same decade.

options.text: Because the cost of holding each territory differed, and the centre could not afford them all.
Because the metropolitan electorate applied the same standard everywhere without exception.
options.misconception: assumes the metropolitan electorate behaved identically everywhere

options.text: Because colonial governors were given written instructions to concede in every case.
options.misconception: invents written instructions ordering concession everywhere

options.text: Because the number of treaties signed with local rulers was identical across territories.
options.misconception: assumes treaty counts were the same in every territory

questions.explanation: Imperial withdrawal was a question of what the centre could afford, so costlier territories were conceded sooner while cheaper ones were held longer. Uniform standards, written instructions and identical treaty counts did not shape the pattern.
questions.hint: Ask what the centre could afford to keep.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how limited violence still produced lasting tenure change.
questions.stem: A research group asks you to explain why the highland rebellion produced lasting changes in land tenure even in districts where violence was limited.

answer.exemplar: Where the administration's grip on land was already thin, a small number of refusals to pay rents or to move off an enclosure was enough to make the ownership question impossible to ignore. Districts that saw little fighting still found their rent rolls under challenge, their labour levies suspended and their claims revised, because once the legal basis of the allocation was questioned, no administrator could enforce it. The absence of large-scale violence therefore says less about the depth of the grievance than about how quickly the colonial state conceded.

questions.explanation: Where the legal basis of land allocation was questioned, enforcement collapsed without violence, so limited fighting did not mean limited grievance. Violence and the depth of the claim were separate variables.
questions.hint: Focus on what happened where there was little violence.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Strategic stakes around the Indian Ocean
questions.learningObjective: Interpret an admiralty letter as customary practice on a shared lane.

stimulus.body: The letter notes that convoys using the eastern route have twice been delayed by escorts diverted to answer a distress call on the northern approaches, and that the merchant captains now sail in company rather than singly. It advises that the station's commanders keep a record of every request for escort and of the time taken to arrive.

questions.stem: An archive gallery uses this letter. What does it show about how the sea route was governed in practice?

options.text: The route worked through negotiated usage and recorded requests rather than fixed rules.
The route was governed by an international code that commanders were obliged to enforce.
options.misconception: invents an international code of navigation binding on commanders

options.text: The route was largely unregulated, because escorts were never dispatched to protect traffic.
options.misconception: reads the letter as evidence escorts were never dispatched

options.text: The route was closed to convoy traffic following the delays described in the letter.
options.misconception: infers a closure of the route from the delays described

questions.explanation: The letter shows practice built from custom, escort requests and written records rather than a binding code, which is how a shared sea lane functioned while sovereignty stayed disputed. No code existed, escorts were dispatched, and the route stayed open.
questions.hint: Ask what the commanders recorded and why.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish legal from economic independence in new states.
questions.stem: A comparative panel asks whether the new Caribbean states were genuinely independent or merely differently governed versions of the old colony.

options.text: The states were not independent in any sense, since the flag changed but nothing else did.
options.misconception: denies the new states any genuine independence whatever

options.text: The states were independent in every sense, because sovereignty covered all aspects of life.
options.misconception: assumes sovereignty extended to every aspect of economic life

options.text: The states were independent in law and government, but not in economic terms.
The states were not independent in law, only in their conduct of foreign affairs.
options.misconception: restricts legal independence to the conduct of foreign affairs

questions.explanation: New constitutions, assemblies and diplomatic representation show real legal independence, while unchanged ownership, credit and trade patterns show economic continuity. Legal and economic sovereignty moved at different speeds.
questions.hint: Ask what changed in law and what did not change.
